passage:
After a video of him slipping in the changing room went round Year 10, Felix stopped eating in the canteen. At home in Bradford, his dad had been out of work since spring.
The only place anyone asked how he was doing was a voice channel on a game server. Older players, patient, funny. "You're one of us, brother." "They laugh at lads like you because they want you small." Nobody explained who "they" were. It didn't matter. For the first time in months, Felix felt part of something.
On Thursday one of them said, "Don't tell your mum about us. She won't get it."
Felix told Liam at the bus stop, half laughing. Liam didn't laugh. "Mate, that's the bit that's wrong."
That evening Felix left the server and told his mum everything. She switched off the kettle and sat down beside him. "Thank you for telling me. You're not in trouble. We'll go into school together tomorrow."

qa.q: Where did anyone ask Felix how he was doing?
qa.a: Only in a voice channel on a game server.

qa.q: What was Felix feeling that made the voice channel so appealing?
qa.a: Felix felt humiliated after the video and unseen at home, so being called "brother" and part of something filled a real hunger to belong.

qa.q: Which moment was the turning point, and what did Felix do right?
qa.a: Being told to hide the group from his mum was the warning sign; Felix left the server and told his mum everything that same evening.

qa.q: How did Felix's mum respond when he told her?
qa.a: She switched off the kettle, sat beside him, thanked him, told him he was not in trouble and planned to go into school with him the next day.

grounding: A humiliated teenage boy is drawn to online voices offering brotherhood and an enemy, and when asked for secrecy he leaves and tells his mum, who responds at once.

passage:
The counsellor's room at Neelam's school smelled of marker pens. Preeti ma'am had seen the slogans in her notebook: "Rise." "They took everything." "Sisters stand together."
"Where did these come from?" she asked, not angrily.
Neelam shrugged, then couldn't stop. How Mr Verma had read her failed maths marks aloud to the whole class in July and everyone laughed. How afterwards she'd found a channel, then a Saturday meeting behind the bus depot. Older girls who called her sister. Who said her anger meant she was awake. Who told her exactly whose fault her life was.
"It's the first time anyone said I matter," Neelam said. Her voice cracked.
Preeti ma'am didn't argue about the slogans. "Being laughed at like that hurts. You deserved better." She pulled a chair closer. "Let's talk about the maths, and about what you'd want to build. And I'll call your mother today so she can help too."

qa.q: What did Mr Verma read aloud to the class?
qa.a: Mr Verma read Neelam's failed maths marks aloud to the whole class.

qa.q: What does Neelam's cracked voice show about what drew her in?
qa.a: It shows the pull was the feeling of mattering after being humiliated, much more than any idea the group preached.

qa.q: What did Preeti ma'am do that kept Neelam talking?
qa.a: Preeti ma'am listened without arguing, named the hurt of being laughed at, and moved to practical help, including calling Neelam's mother that day.

qa.q: What would change if Preeti ma'am had scolded Neelam about the slogans?
qa.a: Neelam would likely have shut down and felt that only the group understood her, making the pull stronger.

grounding: A humiliated teenage girl is pulled to a group offering sisterhood, purpose and someone to blame, and a counsellor responds to the hurt beneath it.

passage:
Friday
Worst day. Sir read my marks out loud and the back row laughed. Then Pranav posted a photo of my torn shoe in the class group.
Came home and watched the channel again. The man in the videos always seems to be talking straight to me. He says guys like us are kept down on purpose by "them", the people who laugh and run everything, and that it's not our fault. He says we're warriors, not losers.
Tonight someone from the comments added me to a group called Brothers. Forty guys. They welcomed me by name. One said, "You're one of us now." I haven't felt that since we moved here.
Minakshi di saw my screen at dinner and asked, "Who are these brothers?" I said nobody. She didn't push, but she sat next to me longer than usual.
I don't even really get what they believe. I just like being someone's brother.
Tanvir

qa.q: What was the group Tanvir was added to called?
qa.a: A group called Brothers.

qa.q: Why do the channel and the group feel so good to Tanvir?
qa.a: Tanvir feels humiliated and alone after the day at school, and the group makes Tanvir feel welcomed and important; the pull is belonging more than any belief.

qa.q: What could Minakshi di do next?
qa.a: Keep sitting with Tanvir, ask gently about the day at school, and bring in a parent or the school counsellor soon, without mocking the group.

qa.q: How might Minakshi di have felt hearing Tanvir's 'nobody'?
qa.a: Minakshi di probably felt worried by the quick answer and chose closeness over an argument, staying beside Tanvir longer than usual.

grounding: Shows a humiliated teenager pulled toward an online voice that names an enemy and offers brotherhood, where belonging matters more than ideas.

passage:
Since his father's shop shut down, Dhruv had stopped going to the kasba school. People stared, or he felt they did. Evenings he sat at the tea stall by the bus stand, where a group of older young men met.
Their leader, a smooth talker with a new motorbike, bought him tea every day. "Your father's shop didn't fail. Outsiders took it. They take everything from people like us." He never said which outsiders, exactly. He didn't need to. He gave Dhruv a job putting up posters and called him "brother" in front of everyone.
Dhruv felt tall for the first time in months.
Then his cousin Keerthana, home from college for the holidays, found him there. She didn't lecture. She said, "The panchayat library needs someone to run the computer class for kids. It pays a little. I told them you're good with phones."
Dhruv looked at the posters in his hand, then at her. "Why me?"
"Because you are," she said.

qa.q: What job did the leader give Dhruv?
qa.a: A job putting up posters.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv feel tall at the tea stall?
qa.a: Dhruv felt respected and proud again after months of shame over the shop, because the leader called him 'brother' in front of everyone.

qa.q: What makes Keerthana's offer a wise response?
qa.a: It offers real purpose and respect, running the computer class, without a lecture, so Dhruv has another place to feel useful.

qa.q: What would change if Keerthana had lectured Dhruv at the tea stall?
qa.a: Dhruv would likely have felt shamed again and moved closer to the group, which was offering respect instead of criticism.

grounding: Shows a teenager ashamed after his family's loss drawn to local voices who blame outsiders and give him a role and brotherhood.

passage: After the video of Yuki tripping in the school corridor went round his class in Osaka, he stopped eating lunch in the cafeteria. At home he stayed up late in a forum where older boys wrote long posts about people like us being laughed at by them, the ones with easy lives. "You're not weak," one wrote to him. "You're awake. You're our brother now." Nobody at school had called Yuki anything but a joke for weeks. The forum had names for everything: the enemy, the plan, the brotherhood. He liked having names. They turned the shame into anger, and anger felt better. One night his older sister Mina, home from university, saw the screen over his shoulder. "Who's them?" she asked. Yuki shrugged. "People who think they're better." Mina didn't argue. She sat on his bed. "Tell me about the video," she said. He was quiet a long time. Then he told her. Later that night she told their mother, and the three of them agreed to see the school counsellor together.

qa.q: What did one forum member call Yuki?
qa.a: Their brother, awake rather than weak.

qa.q: Why did the forum appeal to Yuki?
qa.a: Yuki felt humiliated and alone after the video, and the forum turned that shame into anger and belonging, which felt better.

qa.q: What did Mina do well?
qa.a: She didn't argue about who them was; she sat down, asked about the video to reach the hurt underneath, and brought in their mother and the school counsellor that night.

qa.q: What might Mina have felt seeing the screen?
qa.a: Mina likely felt worried and protective at the talk of an enemy and a brotherhood, but kept calm so Yuki would keep talking.

grounding: Shows a humiliated teenager pulled toward online voices that name an enemy and offer brotherhood, where the draw is belonging more than ideas.
